projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Ralph Beardsley was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Today is September twenty-second, 2007. I am Nolan Smith and I am interviewing Ralph Burt Beardsley at 3530 Rolling Springs Drive. Mr. Beardsley is my interviewee.] Mr. Beardsley is eighty-three years old and was born on August twenty-first, 1924. Mr. Beardsley served in World War II. Mr. Beardsley was in Navy and held the following rank: Lieutenant. Wereyou drafted or did you enlist to fight in WW2?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: I got an appointment.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: an appointment, okay you were appointed to World...

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Senator from Ohio. That's where we were born and raised in Cleveland Heights, OH.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: At that time, were you living here in Indiana or were you living somewhere else at the time?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: When I was appointed, Cleveland Heights, OH.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Why were you appointed? Was there any reason you were appointed?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: I guess I was wanting to go to have additional education but there was an opportunity for a job and also to serve the country.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: If so, why did you enlist? Why did you enlist in the navy? Do you remember anything about your first few days in the military? (third party - you were appointed to go to the academy, is that correct?)

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: That's correct. From the reserve, we got commissioned. And when we went through the actually... the programs were part of military academies were 4 year programs. WW2 only two years okay they moved it up. So when we got out after two years then we had to set for exams of course and during that period we were mid-shipmen and mid-shipmen, by they way, were the ones that get all the dirty jobs. We also while we were at the academy, we went to sea too. We went to sea for I guess it was probably usually six to nine months we went to sea. And that's when I was in [Unintelligible] and I had books to do, you know, at the academy they called it sea books or something like that. You had to keep up on your education and you also were assigned duty on board ship for defense of the ship. Like I happen to be on twenty millimeters and when we would have an attack or we were at a Conway when we had submarines giving us a lot of trouble, we would be up in those mountains and doing those jobs too. So, you know, when we finished that training period at sea then we came back to the academy and we continued on with our education at the academy. And then when we finished that we got commissioned.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Okay. What were your boot camp instructors like?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Boot camp? Good teachers.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: What was the whole boot camp experience like for you?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: You had the upper classmen there that kind of worked on you pretty hard because they had lot of discipline and you did a lot of things for them to because you were just [Unintelligible], those are pretty bad guys. But anyway, we got along okay. And you got to learn to live with other men too, other boys, because we had four in a room. And when you live with four guys in a room you gotta learn how to live together, work together. You couldn't complain to your mother about either because she ain't there.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: I know that you were part of WW2 and the Korean War, but where exactly did you go during these wars?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: While I was still at school or even after?

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Even after.

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Anywhere in the world. I was in the Pacific. I was in the Atlantic, I was up north in the Artie Circle, South America. I was all over the place. We did spend a lot of time down there. I was in London as an example. During the VI 's and the V2's, do you know what those are?

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: No

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Those are bombs that the Germans were shooting from Europe over the channel and into England and they were propelled and they ran out of juice and then they came back and blew up everything. London was washed out almost. And I was in London at that time on a ship. Cause we came in to drop off the stuff that we were bringing over to the English and you know we had rush through etc, etc. and then after we were finished getting rid of our cargo to England and they took off and went to North Africa. We was in the invasion of North Africa. That was against Rommel and his crew of [Unintelligible] and then after left our cargo there then I went back to the academy and that's when I finished my tuition - I mean I graduated at that time in 1944. So I spent the rest of my time at the academy. We didn't go back to sea. But then when we got out of the academy then we went back to sea again. But I was in all of the Pacific, Atlantic, Russia, went all over. And by the way, out casualty rate was about twenty-eight percent. Highest casualty rate of even the marines!

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: How did the cultures differ from what you were used to and was it hard to get used to it?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: What I tell you? I took French in eighth grade, ninth grade, tenth grade, eleventh grade and I thought I could speak French real well. I thought I could get along. What happens when I in the invasion in North Africa, they speak French in Algiers. I said, well, boy I could really make out talking to those people. They can understand me and I can understand them. No how! I couldn't WWll-Beardsley understand them and they couldn't understand me. I still speak a little French. If I want to give some people a hard time, I'll do it in French.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Can you remember your first job or assignment?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: It was probably one of the dirtiest jobs on board ship. I was cleaning bilges. Midshipmen are the scum of the world, everybody is training them, you know, and shouting at us as nothing and we had to even, I'll tell you a story. We were on board ship during World War II on liberty ships. We had no washing machines, you scrubbed your clothes with a scrub board and water of course and salt. There was two of us mid-shipment on board a ship and we decided we gonna do something better than scrub boards, we made a washing machine out of a fifty-five gallon drum. We cut the top out of it then we got two pieces of wood that were three by three and made a cross like that, put a hook on it. Put a line up to the excentric on the main propulsion engine which drove the ship. And it would go up and down about ninety-six a minute, okay. So you didn't leave them there too long because of you did you got a bunch of rags out it. But it was a lot of easier to do that then was the scrub. We didn't have any ... even the officers had to do it that way. Anyway that was kind of interesting. I think that was one of the bad jobs we didn't like. And the other bad job that was on us was cleaning bilges. A bilge on the ship is all the way at the bottom and everything goes there basically, the oils and everything gets swept into it. Sooner or later you got to clean it out, okay. And then you're in there probably in a space that is about this high up off the floor and you're down in there digging this stuff up and getting it out throwing it over the side. And there was some other duties that were always assigned to midshipmen and that would be like when we looking all the time for submarines and we didn't have radar, no radar in those days. And so you'd be up there in the crow's nest which is way on the top up on the ship and kept looking for submarines and you're pretty high up so it goes like this, goes like this.... If you didn't get seasick, you'd get over it pretty quick. That was a bad duty too.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Did you see any combat? What was it like?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Well, normally merchant ships during the war would run in convoys. And what a convoy was, was a bunch of cargo ships or oilers and they would have around them would be destroyers or frigates whatever for protection. Well that protection wasn't too good. Anyway, that's what we would do. And it was very interesting, sometimes, you'd be going like over in the North Atlantic around Nova Scotia in that area. You get up to the Grand Banks and the Grand Banks, you'd be in fog maybe three or four days, you know, you're only going ten knots, that's not very fast. You couldn't understand how those ships would get where they were after the fog lifted because, you know, you didn't have radar, the only thing you had was a pull. They had what they call a scoop and it was like you could pull it through the water and it would take the water and shoot it up in the air. Well the ship behind then could see the spot of water going up in the air they knew they were getting too close. But they was a lot amount of accidents. One time we were up in the Nova Scotia area. There was such a bad fog. It took about three or four days and when it all cleared you looked at the ship ahead of you, one to the right of 'ya, left of 'ya and think, "How the hell did they ever get there?" They weren't there when we started. Lot of them ran into each other too. We did have convoys that were baby ships and they were the ones that were suppose to help protect because we weren't armed with, well, we had some big guns like a five inch gun which was a surface gun and they had twenty millimeter maybe, machine guns.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: What were your most memorable experiences from the war?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Oh I think one of my greatest accomplishments that I had acquired was I took a ship, I navigated a ship without any convoy, an oiler, from New York around the world and took thirteen months and I was navigation officer and I ran it around. We had no convoys 'cause we were high speed. We could get up sixteen to twenty knots so we could run without a convoy. We didn't have to worry about submarines cause you had the kind of speed but if you were ten knots you had a lot of problems. But that was a great accomplishment I thought but that was when I was an office.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Were you a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Okay

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: But I can tell you something about prisoners of war. In Singapore, they were occupied by the Japanese during WWII and they took a lot of prisoners and a lot of Australians were in that area with the British of course. And anyway the war was about getting, well, the war in Europe was over and we were still fighting with the Japanese. So anyway, we were asked to up to China, up to Fu Chow, and pick up some prisoners of war. They were prisoners of war for probably three to four years, they were. They were there and we picked up something like twenty-four, twenty-five and took 'em to Australia to [Unintelligible] and [Unintelligible] and those people were just skin and bones because the Japanese were very, very bad people, prisoners of war. It's a horrible stories that were going on. I could tell you a real nasty one and it's a true story. Yeah we had the Japanese Navy and Army both had officer's clubs just like we had. They would eat there and they had entertainment and all kinds of stuff. Slot machines too by the way, these prisoners of war, but anyway these Japanese officers, one of the delicacies that they thought was very good to have was having liver from the prisoners of war. And that's pretty WWII-Beardsley bad. Batain as you probably know a lot about that one, the March of Batain were they marched them for I don't know how many miles, hundreds of miles with a bayonet.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations? If so, what were they for?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Yeah. The ones that I had were all for areas of combat. In other words if you were in the North Pacific or wherever you were you had different areas, but I never was interned or anything like that. I wasn't captured. I didn't no Congressional Medal of Honor or any of that.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: in the war, how did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Letters. We didn't have telephones then. Maybe we could send them a message by [Unintelligible] if they could understand that.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: How was the food in the military?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Food? We had, well, aboard ship you have enlisted people, okay, and you officers and you had like warrant officers and they would have what they called their mess and that mess was a cooks and they had bakers so forth in their mess which did their cooking and serving. And you had to join it and you had to pay into it 'cause we got paid for food. During World War II, no, but during the Korean War we did. Anyway, you would join the mess and you would have a pot of money and the cooks and so forth would buy the food from the commissary which was military and so they had their own food. Now, the enlisted men that was not true. The food was brought aboard ship and the cooks cooked it and served it and everything else. Now the officers, there was good food, the cooks were a little better but, and, you got a little more ice cream maybe if you had an ice maker on board ship but most of the time we didn't have ice cream or we used to do, we did a lot of playing card duty when I was in the Navy and we would pick up the pilots when they go in a drink and then we would go back on to the carrier and say, "He's okay. Everything's alright. Do you want him back?" And they'd say, "Sure." Twenty gallons of WWII-Beardsley ice cream we don't send it back 'cause we couldn't make ice cream, we didn't have a way to make it but they did. So then we would highline across to the carrier and they went back in the air.... those guys are nuts, those pilots. They'd come crashing the plane into the water and come back onto the carrier and take off at another point.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Were there other supplies?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: They were very limited. You know, you didn't have any, you know, clothing. Or foul weather gear used to be a problem. You never had enough so you had to swap with somebody else that was on the watch, but it wasn't too bad. You had limits to it too. There wasn't a lot of stuff going around and you did a lot of swapping too. You had a lot of something and that guy over there had something you wanted well you'd swap him.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: What were your primary sources for stress or pressure during WW2?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: You used to be able to go and have recreation sometimes but not too often. That would not be too true with the military, the army, those guys but aboard ship you could get into a port somewhere and go to shore and have.... be organized that kind of stuff. But then you had doctors, you know, onboard ship. We used to you know on merchant ships, we had a doctor usually onboard. And of course, military navy ship there were doctors, dentists and such. We had recreation on board as best we could but you know when you're shooting a lot of guns and trying to kill somebody, you didn't take too much time to do that.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Did you have any special rituals or superstitions during the war to give you good luck?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: What was your main source of entertainment in the war?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Oh it would be organized athletic baseball and some football if you could do it. You could do movies, stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Were there any shows or acts that you attended for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Acts? No, I don't think so. We weren't entertainers. By the way, we did have entertainers. The waves, not waves, what did they call them? The women. They used to, the actors went to the basis and entertained the troops. That was going on pretty much when it was possible.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: When you were on leave, what did you do?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Probably went home. We would get some relief and you could something, sports, stuff like that. During the Korean War, not during World War II, but during the Korean War I had my golf clubs onboard ship and we get into a port. I was on destroyers then, we were always with the battle wagons and the carriers and cruisers. We were the little guys, little ships. And we'd go into port, we'd go into a small port because we were a small ship. The big ones went had to go into the big ports. And so we'd get in there and the Mayor would come down and say, "Boys, what would you like to?" And we'd like to say we'd like to golf if we were England or Scotland.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Was there any particularly funny, ironic, or unusual moment in the war?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: I don't think so. And I'll tell you this is a little side story. This was yesterday. I play at Hillcrest and I came in after, I just had a colonoscopy the day before and I had to go to the John after the nine holes so I said to the guys, "I'll be right back. I'm going into the clubhouse." So I go to the clubhouse, go to the men's room, went into the stall and turn the lock on it you know. It would not open! I worked at it and worked at it. And man I'm pounding on the door, you know and pounding. And of course, it's somewhat isolated, you know. But I finally got it open. This is the bad part of it. Then we were all done, we came back in to settle up our debts and so forth. And I got a hold of one of the maintenance guys and I said, "I want you to go in to the John here and I want you to get that thing fixes." So I took him in there and I went in again and turned the damn thing and you know I got locked in again. He was there though. He went and got a screwdriver and got me out. But that would be one of those right?

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Right

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: No we didn't have that. Yeah, I'll tell you one that, what was the one that you were asking about now?

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: What question was I asking?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Was there any particularly funny, ironic, or unusual moment in the war?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Well this was during the war, but it wasn't when we were active, shooting things.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: I am on a ship for sixty days, this was during the war. Sixty day, training ship it was [Unintelligible] in the Spanish American war. That was a pretty long time ago, okay. And it was called the [Unintelligible] and it was in [Unintelligible] and it was steam and sail boats. And in the service you know what the head is? That's the John. And where do you think the head is? It's in the head of the ship. That's where the name came from. And then the bottom of ship they had troughs that ran from the higher level to the lower level and then boards were put on the troughs. I think you used to see them over in the old state parks and so forth. Anyway, they were boards and every morning we had to pick the boards all up and boil them. But anyway some of the mid-shipmen what they would do, they would go up there and they would take some toilet tissue, crush it up and put it in the trough and needless to say the water was running all the time and they would light it. And all these mid-shipment are sitting there going to the John and here comes the paper crumbled up and on fire. That was one of those. You can forget about that one, but it was one I'll never forget. We slept in hammocks too, by the way.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: What were some of the pranks that you played on the others?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: That was one of them. That's a start for ya.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Do you have any photographs or diaries that you kept during the war?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Yeah. Some of them are right here.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Do you ever look back at those?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Yeah, once in a while.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: What did you think of some of your officers or fellow soldiers on your ship?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: There were good ones and there were bad ones. The worst one, I guess the worst one I used to think about is the Warrant Officers. These guys were chief warrants and they'd been in the Navy a long time and they would be the laziest persons in the world. They would always sit in their quarters, not quarters, but their dining facilities and drink coffee. Then the Chief Petty Officer, not the warrants, the petty officers, who reported to the warrants, would be doing all the work and the warrant officers would sit there and play cards or tell jokes so we used to give them a hard time. And I happen to be a Division Officer at the time and I used to give them a hard time too. I went after the warrants. We had some incompetent ones too. Especially in regards to this one and regards to [Unintelligible]. I'll never forget I had a captain on one of the ships I was one. He graduated from Annapolis and he was a full commander, he was captain of the ship but 11 WWII-Beardsley he was full commander and he was the worst seaman in the world. He would have a ship, the most maneuverable ship in the Navy. We had, there was 2600 ton, which is a pretty good size, about 300 feet, a little over. We had 80,000 horsepower, okay? That's a lot of stuff. We had twin screws and we had twin rudders. We didn't have any thrusters because they didn't have them back in those days. And you could maneuver with that kind of facilities you could just pull it along side of a dock, except this guy. And I used to be on the bough of the ship when we come into port. And I had all my lines, you know the lines that they tie up with. I had them all doubled up. In other words, they were twice as long as would be normal that was because he never got that close to the dock. And I had line throwing guns which was a small gun that you would shoot and you had a line hooked to it and the projector would go and that would shoot quite a little way and then they could pick that up and that would be hooked to the big lines and they could pull them. I had mine, I had a cannon up there. A small cannon because I'd never got close enough cause I could throw it that far. But he was one of the worse. He was a nice guy but he wasn't competent.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Do you remember the time when you service ended?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: When I got out? Yeah. My parents came to New York and I got in their car and went home. And that was a real trip too. I'll never forget that because, you know, during the war they didn't build automobile. And my dad had a 1940 maybe Buick and so they came up there to New York and then we went home and on the turnpike I think we stopped at every stream to get water because the radiator was boiling over and the tires were all retreads. They put another tread on it and they were always blowing out or going flat. I mean it was a bad trip. Trains were another problem when you would be on leave or something like. We went on trains or buses but trains used to be terrible during the war. There was no heat in them, it was bad.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Was it hard to get back into the flow of normal life after the war, what was that like?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Got married. Ha ha. I got married in 1946. Came home from New York and then I got married shortly afterwards. I had been still married to her sixty-one years. Started going with her in 1939. When we were, our families belong to the same church and I was president of Young People and she was my secretary. We have a long time together and still going. By the way, she graduated. It was interesting my wife, she was a pretty smart women. But she went to college after she went to school and I was gone. I was at the Academy. So she went to Allegany College up in New York and she spent there a year and then she decided she was going.. .she went into Red Cross and was a volunteer during the war. Then we got married after the war, she didn't have the opportunity.....anyway, she went back. We moved to York, PA. She decided to go back to school. This was 1968. She said, "I'm going to go back to school." Of course, the kids were grown, they were out of high school. So anyway she went back to Penn State, she graduated in 1970. Cum Laude! Yeah, she's something. Okay.

sp.speaker: Nolan Smith
sp.p: Did you return to work and what was your career?

sp.speaker: Ralph Beardsley
sp.p: Yeah. I did. Let's see that would be 1946. My sister who was working at Thompson Products which was TRW, do you know TRW. Well, they're a big outfit and they had a plant up in Lafayette too and they still have a plant up in Lafayette. But anyway, she had some influence and she got a job for me. Which is kind of interesting. But anyway, I went to work in 1946 in the engineering department and at that time I didn't have a degree because two years at the Academy didn't have enough credit. So anyway, I started work there - that was in 1946 at $150 a month. Okay? At that time, married now, okay and I went to John Carroll in Cleveland.. .or University Heights. Good Jesuit school. I was carrying at work, working 8 hours a day and I was going to John Carroll and carrying twenty-one hours. We went to school on Saturdays too. But anyway, I got enough credits and then I got my diploma from the Academy. That was kind of interesting. But anyway, I worked my way through and at that time in 1946 we had bought all of the buildings that were there were all owned by the government - World War II. So we decided, the owners, decided to buy the buildings and that's what we did and we were doing $200 million dollars a year in business. Okay. I left. I worked for that company for twenty years and I went from that drawing board to a vice president and we had more fun and when I left we were doing eight billion in sales. So we had, we did have a ball, I mean a ball. When companies grow that kind, that opportunities for everybody in that company were, you know, everybody moved on. So anyway, that's what I did. And then after I left TIW I had one of those Chief Warrant Officers I think that was a president of a division and I had at that time I was a manufacturing manager of all manufacturing and I told him I said, "I think I'd like to have more responsibility and I know I can go to another division because I know everybody there. Move up in the organization." He goes, "Uh-uh. I need you here." And so I go "Well, I guess I have to go someplace else then." And so I did. I left town and went with another company and I was a vice president. Of uh, Diamond Chain. Did ya hear of Diamond Chain? Do you? They don't make diamonds for ladies fingers here. But anyway, we've been in business now 115 years here in Indianapolis. That's a long time. You're not gonna find many companies around that long. But it's part of Hamstead Industries which is in Chicago. We have a number of divisions there. Lot of.. .heavy in the rail industry. Here we make link chain basically. We supply the chains for the Wilbur Wright's Kitty Hawk. We supplied the chain for that, in fact, we just made some not too long ago for that new one that they just built. I don't know where they're putting it, it may be over in Dayton. But anyway, we supply a lot of the convey for the Gatlin guns and we... they're big stuff. They go up to thirty mill there, which is a pretty good size and we're feeding..... (Tape stopped recording here. Refer to revised edition for the veterans full answers to the following questions.)
